lesson.title: Volts per Division: Scaling a Signal to Fit the Screen
lesson.summary: Vertical sensitivity sets how many volts each vertical division on the oscilloscope screen represents, letting you read a signal's amplitude directly off the display the same way the time base lets you read its period.
lesson.body:
If the time base is the ruler for the horizontal axis, vertical sensitivity is the ruler for the vertical one. It is a control, again usually a knob with a one, two, five sequence of steps, that sets how many volts each vertical division on the grid represents. Just as the sweep rate does not touch the actual signal, the vertical sensitivity setting does not change the voltage coming out of your circuit, it only changes how much of the screen a given voltage swing occupies.

The reason this matters connects directly to amplitude. A signal's amplitude can be described a few different ways: as a peak value measured from a center reference, or as a peak to peak value measured from the very bottom of the swing to the very top. An oscilloscope screen is naturally suited to measuring peak to peak amplitude, because you can simply count how many vertical divisions the waveform spans from its lowest point to its highest point, then multiply by the volts per division setting. Suppose the sensitivity is set to 2 volts per division, and a sine wave's trace spans 3 divisions from its bottom to its top. The peak to peak amplitude is 3 divisions times 2 volts per division, which is 6 volts peak to peak. If that waveform is centered on zero volts, as most AC signals are when viewed this way, the peak amplitude on either side of center is half of that, or 3 volts.

Choosing the right sensitivity is a balancing act very similar to choosing the right time base. Set it too coarse, with too many volts packed into each division, and a small signal collapses into a thin, hard to read line near the middle of the screen, throwing away vertical resolution exactly where you need precision. Set it too fine, with too few volts per division, and a larger signal runs off the top and bottom edges of the display entirely, a condition called clipping or overrange on the screen, which is not the same thing as clipping in the circuit itself but will just as thoroughly ruin your reading. The goal, much like with the time base, is to pick a setting that lets the waveform fill a generous portion of the screen without running off it.

Time base and vertical sensitivity work together, not separately. The time base decides how wide your window into the signal's history is, the vertical sensitivity decides how much of the screen's height that signal's swing occupies. A well framed waveform, one that shows several clean cycles at a comfortable height, is the product of having both controls set thoughtfully, and it is the starting point for every other measurement discussed in the chapters that follow, including the coupling choices covered next.
